Why do people still like Bernie?

When you look back on what Bernie has done in the congress for the last 20 years he has been correct about a lot of issues. He is a smart guy that has been on the side of the people for a long time. I can't get into his head space about why he chose to campaign so hard for Hillary, but I imagine that running for President and getting 50% of a political party to vote for you does something to your psyche. I personally discovered Bernie when I was protesting at Occupy LA and he made an impact on my political life then.

Bernie's message wasn't free everything, it was about spending federal dollars on things that people need. Oil subsidies and fighter planes don't educate kids or pave the roads. Breaking up big banks makes banks go out and find people to take out loans. The free market isn't about locking up public money and then wait for multinationals to come to in the front door. Bernie wants people to work, but unlike the political elites, he wants the people to get paid more.

A lot of it boils down to wanting "free" needs. In theory it still makes sense to many people. If we all need it, wouldn't it be more cost effective to all pool together rather than pay more individually? There are also plenty of studies that show how much better society gets when everyone has reached a certain sweet spot (that sweet spot the average person would be in if wages kept up with inflation). Crime goes down, violence goes down, suicide goes down, all those expensive negatives drop and all the happiness levels are good things go up. Isn't it more cost effective to get everyone to that point rather than eternally pay for the negative effects?

It falls apart very quickly once you really start digging into things and realize not everyone is compatible with that system.

Socialism(ish) systems just fit some people. Personally, I would prefer an Amish styled society with technology. Society is ultimately just a collection of things needing to get done. Anyone who puts in the work to do the work, gets the benefits of society. A simple meritocracy. But what do you do with those who don't put in the work (whether due to laziness or physical inability)? Kick them out or take care of them? How do you motivate people to go above and beyond? Have an encouragement program depending on society's needs? (is that fair to those who helped without needing those encouragements?) or simply hope the passionate fill the gaps? Once you really dig into the details, even I have a hard time justifying it over the capitalist system that really does just self adjust to society's needs and accommodates all types. If you are more socialist/communist or just want at cost needs, a free market of non-profit companies is perfect. Capitalism is still a meritocracy in most ways. Some may not like how money takes more of a priority than human lives, happiness, survival, and quality of life... but money is the best way to balance things out.

Socialism just has a very nice simplicity to it. Focusing more on actually living our lives not just surviving. We only spend 1/4th of our lives actually enjoying/living our life, the rest is sleeping, working, and maintenance. That doesn't feel like freedom. But we're we in a Star Trek socialist society where money/jobs weren't a necessity for survival, we would have the freedom to live our one short life however we wished. That's super tempting.

That said Sanders was/is a shit socialist. Like most social programs they are really just forced monopolies. He just wanted to expand over priced wasteful as fuck systems. If he came out with plans that really bottomed dollar the system while increasing its effectiveness, people would feel very different about paying for it. But we are swimming in entitlement debt and be just wanted to increase taxes so we can write private monopolies even bigger blank checks.

As for the wealth redistribution, a lot of people feel like the system has already redistributed the wealth and it is unsustainably unbalanced. 01% of the population can't hold 90% of the wealth, it needs to circulate. The Fed needs to stop stacking the deck.

So I can understand the appeal, I just don't agree with the methods. Really we just need more non-profit competition and open-source more systems to really find the most efficient way to accomplish the task. What is the best way to feed a population, what is the best way to educate a population, what is the best way to make that sweet spot of quality of life as attainable as possible. Right now we kinda suck ass at all of that. Doing very well, compared to most countries but all falling short. The system is kinda shitty but Sanders didn't want to fix the system, just expand the taxes to pay for them.

One other thing that gave me a nice red pill moment. Public education, we already have "free" education that isn't being utilized. We can't force everyone to follow the most practical path. There was a school in my area that completely collapsed. It had all the funding it needed, but students didn't give a shit and parents didn't give a shit. Why fund a program, no one will actually use, is terribly wasteful, or just not doing a good job accomplishing the task?

I have watched him lob grenades at many of the issues for lots of years. I work in the housing filed in LA and know that there is no such thing as a "free" market b/c e.g. the Irvine Co. owns 80% of the remaining developable land in the OC. Lots of developers take advantage of governmental subsidies and then don't actually meet the low/moderate income housing need. The City fo Huntington Beach demolished a mobile home park, spent $50 Mill in supposed Low/mod income housing funds to acquire and assemble prime coastal land and then "sold" it to the Huntington Waterfront Hilton for $1 with promises of employee/affordable housing opportunities. Yeah, right. Anyway, enough rant, here is Bernie's story from when he was Mayor of Burlington where he actually made the developers trickle the money down to the people:

In 1986 when Bernie Sanders, then the mayor of Burlington, Vermont, confronted the owners of the city’s largest affordable-housing complex. The federal program that had subsidized the Northgate Apartments for 20 years had a loophole that allowed the landlords to convert the buildings into market rentals or luxury condos.

“Bernie pounded his fist on the conference table in his office and told the owners, ‘Over my dead body are you going to displace 336 working families. You are not going to convert Northgate into luxury housing,’” recalled Davis, who was Sanders’s key housing aide.

Under Sanders’s leadership, the city adopted a number of laws to stifle the owners’ plans. One ordinance required apartment owners to give residents two years’ notice before a condo conversion. Others gave residents a pre-emptive right to buy the units and prohibited landlords from bulldozing buildings unless they replaced them with the same number of affordable units. (These measures lowered the selling price of the property.) Sanders then worked with the state government and Senator Patrick Leahy to get the $12 million needed to purchase and rehabilitate the buildings. The city allocated funds to help the tenants hire an organizer, form the Northgate Residents Association, and start the process of converting the complex to resident ownership. Today, Northgate Apartments is owned by the tenants and has long-term restrictions to keep the buildings affordable for working families.

The battle over Northgate Apartments illustrates Sanders’s general approach to governing. In addressing this and many other issues, he encouraged grassroots organizing, adopted local laws to protect the vulnerable, challenged the city’s business power brokers, and worked collaboratively with other politicians to create a more livable city.
